prompt: Why does `total.test.js` live in `unit/` rather than in `tests/`?

choices.text: Node refuses to run a file inside a folder called `tests`
choices.why: Node runs it from anywhere; the trouble is the other runner.

choices.text: Playwright would pick it up as one of its own
choices.why: Right. Playwright runs every `.test.js` and `.spec.js` in `tests/`, and a Node test is not a Playwright test.

choices.text: Unit tests have to sit beside the code they import
choices.why: It imports `../app/store.js` from its own folder; nothing requires it to sit beside the file.

choices.text: To keep it out of the shop's `webServer`
choices.why: `webServer` starts the shop for Playwright; it does not read test folders.

prompt: With `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` pointing at an empty folder, the API test passed and the browser test failed in 2 ms. What does that show?

choices.text: The API test is flaky and happened to pass
choices.why: It passed in every run of the lesson; the folder removed something it never used.

choices.text: Playwright skipped the API test
choices.why: It ran and passed, with a time beside it, in 55 ms.

choices.text: The browser test has a bug in the locator it uses for the banana card
choices.why: It failed launching the browser, before any locator ran.

choices.text: A test that asks only for `request` never starts a browser
choices.why: Right. The browser is started only for a test that asks for a page.

prompt: A Playwright test that sends HTTP calls without opening any page asks only for the ___ fixture.
With `/ 100` removed from the page's `showBasket`, which of the three tests failed?

choices.text: The unit test, because the total was wrong
choices.why: `total()` still returned 590 cents, which is right.

choices.text: The API test, because the JSON changed
choices.why: The server still answered `total: 590`; the change was in the page.

choices.text: Only the browser test, which read R$ 590,00
choices.why: Right. Only the test that reads what the page draws runs the page's code.

choices.text: All three, since they check the same fact
choices.why: They check the same fact through different parts of the shop, and two of those parts were fine.

prompt: `total()` stopped multiplying by the quantity, and the browser test stayed green. Why?

choices.text: It bought just one banana
choices.why: Right. With a quantity of one the defect has no effect; catching it there takes several clicks, and the unit case took one line.

choices.text: The browser cached the old version of `app/store.js`
choices.why: `store.js` runs in the server; the browser never downloads it.

choices.text: `toHaveText` ignores numbers
choices.why: It compares the text, digits included; it caught R$ 590,00 in the other defect.

choices.text: The server was not restarted after the edit
choices.why: Playwright's `webServer` started a fresh shop for the run, and the unit test also read the changed file.

prompt: A change makes `POST /api/basket` ignore the `id` it is sent and always add a banana. Which of this lesson's three tests would fail?

choices.text: The unit test, since the basket is wrong
choices.why: The unit test calls `total()` with lines it builds itself; it never goes through the route.

choices.text: The browser test, since it runs everything
choices.why: It runs the route, but it asks for a banana, and a banana is what it gets.

choices.text: The API test, since it checks the route's answer
choices.why: It checks the answer to a banana, which is still right.

choices.text: None of the three: each one adds a banana
choices.why: Right. Running a layer is not the same as checking it; a test of a mango at either upper layer would catch it.

prompt: At the 281 ms the browser test took, how many seconds would 200 such tests take on one worker?
hint: Multiply the count by the time in seconds.

prompt: Twenty repetitions of the API test took 17.531 s, though one run of the test took 51 ms. Where did the rest go?

choices.text: Into the dot reporter, which is slower than list
choices.why: A reporter prints one character per test; that is not seconds of work.

choices.text: Into a fresh worker process for every repetition
choices.why: Right. The JSON report showed worker 0, 1 and 2 for three repetitions.

choices.text: Into restarting the shop between repetitions
choices.why: `webServer` starts the shop once per run of the command, not per test.

choices.text: Into the browser, which the API test also opened and closed each time
choices.why: The API test ran with no browser on the machine at all.

prompt: A browser test passed 20 runs out of 20. A colleague concludes it is not flaky. What does the lesson's arithmetic say?

choices.text: He is right: 20 is the usual threshold for flakiness
choices.why: There is no such threshold; the question is what a clean twenty rules out.

choices.text: Only a run of 1,000 can show anything
choices.why: Twenty runs do show something: they rule out a test that fails often. They cannot rule out a rare one.

choices.text: A clean twenty is weak evidence
choices.why: Right. A test failing 1 run in 100 passes 20 in a row with probability 0.99 to the power 20, about 0.82.

choices.text: Flakiness belongs to the API layer, not to the browser
choices.why: The browser layer has the most sources of it: a browser, scripts, events and waits.

prompt: The button's text changed from "Add to basket" to "Add to cart". What happened to the tests, and why does it count as a cost?

choices.text: Both Playwright tests failed, so the change was a defect
choices.why: The API test passed; it does not know what the button says.

choices.text: Nothing failed, because locators find buttons by role
choices.why: The locator names the role and the text, and the text changed.

choices.text: The browser test failed after 30 s on a shop that works
choices.why: Right. A change of words is work for every browser test that names them, with no defect behind it.

choices.text: The unit test failed, because `total()` reads the label
choices.why: `total()` knows only ids, prices and quantities.

prompt: What does the test pyramid say about the browser layer?

choices.text: That it should hold 10 per cent of the tests
choices.why: That split came from a blog post as a starting point; the drawing itself fixes no ratio.

choices.text: That it should be narrow, because each test there costs the most
choices.why: Right. The claim is about cost per test; how narrow is left to you.

choices.text: That it can be skipped once the unit tests are thorough
choices.why: The top is narrow, not empty: unit tests cannot see the seam between page and server.

choices.text: That it should run only before a release
choices.why: The pyramid is about how many tests sit at each layer, not when they run.

prompt: Where do the pyramid and the testing trophy disagree?

choices.text: At the top: the trophy wants many more end-to-end tests than the pyramid
choices.why: The trophy's end-to-end cup is small too; the two agree about the top.

choices.text: On whether tests should be automated
choices.why: Both are drawings of automated suites; the cone's manual scoop is the odd one.

choices.text: In the middle: the trophy widens the integration band
choices.why: Right. It bets that a front end's defects live where pieces fit together.

choices.text: At the base: the trophy has no unit tests
choices.why: It keeps a small unit layer, above a base of static checks.

prompt: A team's product is a front end that mostly calls other services and holds almost no rules of its own. Going by this lesson, which shape fits its evidence best?

choices.text: A wide base of unit tests, since the base is always cheapest
choices.why: Cheap, but its defects live in seams that unit tests do not cross.

choices.text: A wide middle, with a small top
choices.why: Right. Defects in the fit between pieces want the band that tests pieces together; the top stays small in every shape.

choices.text: The ice-cream cone, since the browser sees the integration
choices.why: It does, at the highest price per test, for checks a cheaper middle layer could make.

choices.text: No automation at all, as there are no rules to check
choices.why: No rules does not mean no defects: the seams still break.

prompt: Match each check on quitanda to the cheapest layer that can see it.

pairs.left: Three bananas and two guavas cost 4350 cents
The HTML of `/ssr` names every product
pairs.right: an HTTP request for the page

prompt: Lesson 6's request test of `/ssr` passed while the page's buttons did nothing. What does that case teach about moving a check down a layer?

choices.text: That request tests are unreliable and should be avoided
choices.why: It was right about what it checked, the HTML; it just could not see the seam.

choices.text: Nothing: it was a flaky run
choices.why: It passed every time; the defect was outside what it could see, not random.

choices.text: That the check should have been moved further down, to a unit test
choices.why: Lower still sees less of the seam, not more.

choices.text: A lower check keeps its subject and loses the seam
choices.why: Right. If the seam was the subject, at least one browser test has to stay over it.

prompt: A product owner asks for a browser test of every product with every quantity from 0 to 3. What does the lesson suggest instead?

choices.text: Run them all in the browser, but in parallel on more workers
choices.why: Parallel runs divide the hours by the workers; they do not make the browser the right layer for arithmetic.

choices.text: The combinations as unit cases, and one browser journey
choices.why: Right. The arithmetic goes where it is cheap, and one test keeps the seam covered.

choices.text: A random sample of twenty baskets in the browser, a new one each run
choices.why: A random sample tests a different basket each run, which makes a failure hard to reproduce; the rule still belongs below.

choices.text: No test, because the rule is too simple to fail
choices.why: This lesson broke it with one deleted multiplication.

prompt: Put these measured runs in order, quickest first.
items: One run of the API test file
One run of the browser test file
Twenty repetitions of the browser test file
trap: A single run of the two Playwright files differs by about a tenth of a second; the per-test gap only shows across many runs.

prompt: The shop adds a rule: every third pineapple in a basket is free. Where do this lesson's arguments put its tests?

choices.text: A browser test per quantity, since customers see the price
choices.why: Each quantity is a case of arithmetic; at the top each costs a browser and several clicks.

choices.text: Unit cases for the rule, and the journey checks one free pineapple
choices.why: Right. The rule goes where cases are cheap; one browser test shows the discount reaches the screen.

choices.text: Only API tests, since the server computes the total
choices.why: The API layer can check it, but the page still has to draw the new total, which only a browser sees.

choices.text: No tests until a customer reports a wrong price
choices.why: The arithmetic of `total()` broke in this lesson with one deleted multiplication.

prompt: Which question does the lesson ask of a check before it is written as a browser test?

choices.text: Is it what a customer would do?
choices.why: Customers do arithmetic too, through the page; that alone does not earn the browser.

choices.text: Could a cheaper layer see this?
choices.why: Right. If yes it goes down; if no, the browser has earned it.

choices.text: Will it run in under a second on one worker?
choices.why: Speed is a cost, not the test of where a check belongs.

choices.text: Has the page object for this screen been written yet?
choices.why: A page object lowers the cost of a browser test; it does not decide whether one is needed.
